demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette:
Omar, a 78-year-old environmental scientist who had spent his life mapping the slow, predictable cycles of the natural world, now found his own life governed by a terrifyingly abrupt and unpredictable one. It had been six months since the fieldwork expedition he was leading in the Rockies. He had been mentoring a promising graduate student, a young man full of energy, during a high-altitude survey. Omar had pushed the pace, eager to collect the samples before an incoming weather system. He still saw the boy stumbling, gasping for air as his asthma, triggered by the altitude and exertion, spiraled out of control. Omar, panicked and miles from help, made a series of what he now knew were catastrophic errors. The memory of the boy’s desperate, ragged breathing as he collapsed was the sound that now defined Omar’s world.

The aftermath of the accident, which left the student with a permanent hypoxic brain injury, had shattered Omar’s carefully constructed sense of competence and self. The intrusive recollections began soon after. These were not simple memories; they were visceral reenactments. He would be sitting in his study, the quiet hum of his computer a familiar comfort, when the sound of his wife’s heavy breathing from the next room would catch his ear. This seemingly innocuous sound would instantly transport him back to the cold, thin air of the mountain pass. The memory would crash over him with such force that he felt the biting wind on his face and heard the frantic, failing breaths of his student as if it were all happening again, right there in his quiet suburban home. He would grip the arms of his chair, his own breathing hitched, feeling the same gut-wrenching helplessness.

This powerful link between a simple trigger and the re-experiencing of the trauma became the central organizing principle of his suffering. Any flicker of positive emotion was immediately extinguished by it. Last month, at his granddaughter’s birthday party, he had felt a moment of genuine joy watching her blow out the candles on her cake. The warmth of that happiness, however, felt like a profound betrayal. The feeling of contentment itself was the trigger. In an instant, the memory ambushed him: the boy’s face, the fading light in his eyes. The world of the party—the laughter, the bright colours—would recede, replaced by the grey rock and the sickening realization of his failure. He had to excuse himself, retreating to the bathroom, unable to bear the juxtaposition of his family’s happiness with the ruin he felt he had caused.

His wife, Layla, noticed his withdrawal but could not understand its source. Her attempts at comfort only made things worse. An affectionate hug or a hand on his shoulder, meant to soothe, would instead trigger the memory of holding the student, the boy’s body limp in his arms. The physical expression of love became inextricably linked to the tactile memory of his greatest failure. In response to her touch, he would flinch and pull away, leaving a chasm of hurt and confusion between them. Over the months, this cycle calcified. He stopped going on his beloved walks in the local nature preserve. He declined invitations from friends. His world shrank to the four walls of his house, a fortress that failed to keep the true enemy—his own memory—at bay.

When he tries to speak of it, the words evaporate. He knows precisely what happened—every decision, every panicked second—but when he opens his mouth to explain it to Layla, the narrative crumbles. It’s a story made of pure sensation, not language. Afterwards, a profound sense of derealization sets in. The event feels so monstrous, so antithetical to the man he believed himself to be, that it seems impossible it could have actually happened. It feels like a horrific film he was forced to watch, not a chapter of his own life. It was after a particularly harrowing night, when the sound of his own breathing in the dark had trapped him in the memory for nearly an hour, that he finally agreed to seek help. He came to therapy not with a clear goal, but with a quiet, desperate plea: to make the story feel real enough to be spoken, and distant enough to be survived.
